questions.solution:
(2,-1, $\sqrt{\lambda}) are the direction ratios perpendicular to the plane. $(1,2,2)$ is the direction ratio of the line. Then, \vec{l}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{p}=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\sqrt{\lambda} \hat{k}$
Since, $\sin \theta=\frac{\vec{l} \cdot \vec{p}}{|\vec{l}| \cdot|\vec{p}|}=\frac{2-2+2 \sqrt{\lambda}}{3 \times \sqrt{5+\lambda}}\Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{2 \sqrt{\lambda}}{3 \sqrt{5+\lambda}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}} \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}}\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}} \Rightarrow 5+\lambda=4 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{5}{3}$.

Given two planes are 2 x+y+z+1=0 and $2 x+y+z+\alpha=0$

The vector equation of a plane passing through the point $2 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and the line of intersection of the planes r. $(\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})=5$ and $\vec{r} \cdot(3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2 \hat{k})=7$
questions.solution:
Given, planes are

$\vec{r} \cdot(\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})=5
...(i)
and \vec{r} \cdot(3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2 \hat{k})=7$...(ii)
Hence equation of plane passing through the line of intersection of the plane, (i) and plane (ii) is given by

$$\begin{aligned}& \vec{r}_1 \cdot\left(\vec{m}_1+\lambda \vec{m}_2\right)=q_1+\lambda q_2, \lambda \in \mathbb{R} \\
\Rightarrow & \vec{r} \cdot[(\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})+\lambda(3 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2 \hat{k})]=5+\lambda(7) \\
\Rightarrow & \vec{r} \cdot[\hat{i}(1+3 \lambda)+\hat{j}(-2+\lambda)+\hat{k}(3-2 \lambda)]=5+7 \lambda
\end{aligned}$$ 
...(iii)

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{ but given that } \vec{r}=(2 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}) \\
& \Rightarrow 2(1+3 \lambda)+(-3)(-2+\lambda)+(1)(3-2 \lambda)=5+7 \lambda \\
& \Rightarrow 11+\lambda=5+7 \lambda \Rightarrow 6 \lambda=6 \Rightarrow \lambda=1.
\end{aligned}$$  

putting \lambda=1$ in equation (iii), we get

\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \quad \vec{r} \cdot[\hat{i}(1+3)+\hat{j}(-2+1)+\hat{k}(3-2)]=5+7 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \vec{r} \cdot[4 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}]=12

$

questions.solution:
Step-1 Using mid point concept:
Given that the equation of the plane is $a x+b y+c z+d=0$ and the line passed the plane having the coordinates as $P(4,-3,1) and Q(2,3,-5)$.
Let $M(x, y, z)$ be the mid-point of the line passing through the plane. Using the mid-point formula find the coordinate of $M(x, y, z)$.
$x=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x=\frac{4+2}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{6}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow x=3\end{aligned}$ And $\begin{aligned} y & =\frac{y_1+y_2}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =\frac{-3+3}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =\frac{0}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =0\end{aligned}
And
\begin{aligned} z & =\frac{z_1+z_2}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =\frac{1-5}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =\frac{-4}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =-2\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the mid-point $M(x, y, z)$ is obtained as $(3,0,-2)$.
Step-2 : Normal vector to the plane:
The normal of the plane $P Q$ is determined as, $P Q=-2 i+6 j-6 k$
[where coefficient of $i=2-4$, coefficient of $j=3-(-3)$, coefficient of $k=-5-1$]
Then the value of $a$ is $-2, b$ is 6 and $c$ is -6 .
Now the equation of plane is $-2 x+6 y-6 z+d=0$
Using the mid-point coordinate $(3,0,-2)$ finding the value of $d$.
$-2(3)+6(0)-6(-2)+d=0\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & & -6+0+12+d & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & 6+d & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & d & =-6\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the equation of the plane is $-2 x+6 y-6 z+-6=0$.
$\Rightarrow x-3 y+3 z+3=0 \quad$ [equation is of the form ax + by $+\mathbf{c z}+\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}]$
Now substitute the values of $a$ as $1, b$ as $-3, c$ as 3 and $d$ as 3 in
$\begin{aligned}& \left(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\right) . \\&a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=(1)^2+(-3)^2+(3)^2+(3)^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =1+9+9+9 \\ & =28\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the minimum value of $\left(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\right)$ is 28

$y -$coordinate $= - 2$ (z$ coordinate of $P$)

So by perpendicular distance formula we get,

$\left|\dfrac{d}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {2}^{2}}\right| = \dfrac{1}{3} ⇒ d = 1$

So, equation of plane will be~$x + 2y + 2z - 1 = 0$

Now comparing equation of plane with~$x + py + qz + r = 0$

We get,~$p = 2, q = 2 & r = - 1$

So, the value of~$\sqrt{p^{2} + q^{2} + r^{2}} = \sqrt{{2}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$

If the $y$-intercept of the plane $\pi$ is negative and the $z$-intercept is positive then its $y$-intercept is
questions.solution:
Let the equation of plane be

$\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$

Now given~$a = \dfrac{5}{2}$

So, equation becomes~$\dfrac{2x}{5} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$

Now given plane passes through $\left(1, 1, 1\right)$~

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

Now given distance from origin is $\dfrac{5}{7}$

So~ by formula we get,& $\left|\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{4}{25} + \dfrac{1}{b2} + \dfrac{1}{c2}}\right| = \dfrac{5}{7}$

$⇒ \left|\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{25} + \left(\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c}\right)2 - \dfrac{2}{bc}}\right| = \dfrac{7}{5}$

Now using value of~$\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}$~we get,

$⇒ bc = - \dfrac{25}{18} . . . \left(1\right)

&~\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}⇒ \dfrac{b + c}{bc} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$⇒ b + c = - \dfrac{5}{6}$ . . .$\left(2\right)$

Now equation (1) & (2) we get,~

$⇒ b - \dfrac{25}{18b} = \dfrac{- 5}{6}$

$⇒ 18b^{2} + 15b - 25 = 0$

$⇒ \left(6b - 5\right)\left(3b + 5\right) = 0$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{5}{6}$ or $- \dfrac{5}{3}$

So $b = - \dfrac{5}{3}$ {as given $y$ intercept is negative}

Similarly, for second line $\overset{→}{r} \times \overset{→}{b} = \overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}$

The Equation of line is $\overset{→}{r} = \overset{→}{b} + q\overset{→}{a}$

As they both intersect $\overset{→}{b} + q\overset{→}{a} = \overset{→}{b} + p\overset{→}{a}$

On comparing the coefficients we get $p = q = 1$

Hence, the equation of line is $\overset{→}{r} = \overset{→}{b} + \overset{→}{a}$

$⇒ \overset{→}{r} = \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}$

questions.q: $A ( 2, 3, 4 ) , B ( 4, 5, 7 ) , C ( 2, - 6, 3 ) , D ( 4, - 4, k )$ are four points. If the line $\overset{¯}{AB}$ is parallel to $\overset{¯}{CD}$ then $k$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\overset{→}{AB} = \left(4 - 2\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left(5 - 3\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(7 - 4\right)\overset{^}{k} = 2\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}$

Direction ratios $\left<2, 2, 3\right>$

$\overset{→}{CD} = 2\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + ( k - 3 ) \overset{^}{k}$

Direction ratios $\left<2, 2, k - 3\right>$

For $AB$ to be parallel to $CD$, the modulus of their direction cosines should be equal.

Direction cosines of $AB$ will be $\left(\dfrac{2}{17}, \dfrac{2}{17}, \dfrac{3}{17}\right)$

And of $CD$ will be $\left(\dfrac{2}{8 + \left($ k - 3\right)2}, $\dfrac{2}{8 + \left($ k - 3\right)2}$,\dfrac{k - 3}{8 + \left(k - 3\right)2}\right)$

So,

$\dfrac{2}{17} = \left|\dfrac{2}{8 + \left(k - 3\right)2}\right|$

$⇒ 17 = 8 + \left($ k - 3\right)2$

$⇒ 9 = k^{2} + 9 - 6k$

$⇒ $k\left($k - 6\right) = 0$

$⇒ k = 6$

$

questions.solution:
Given, the direction cosines of two lines are& $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$~and& $\left(\dfrac{5}{13}, \dfrac{12}{13}, 0\right) .

We know that,$ the direction ratios of the line bisecting the angle between the lines whose direction cosines are~$\left({l}_{1}, {m}_{1}, {n}_{1}\right)$~and& $\left({l}_{2}, {m}_{2}, {n}_{2}\right)$~are proportional to& $⟨ {l}_{1} + {l}_{2}, {m}_{1} + {m}_{2}, {n}_{1} + {n}_{2} ⟩ .

Hence, the required direction ratios are proportional to~$⟨ $\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{5}{13}$, $\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{12}{13}$, $\dfrac{1}{3} +$0 ⟩ = ⟨ $\dfrac{41}{39}$, $\dfrac{62}{39}$, $\dfrac{13}{39}$ ⟩ .

Thus, the direction ratios are~$⟨ 41, 62, 13 ⟩ .

$

questions.q: Let ${L}_{1}$ (respectively ${L}_{2}$ ) be the line passing through $2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$ (respectively $2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$) and parallel to $3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$ (respectively $\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$). Then the shortest distance between the lines ${L}_{1}$ and ${L}_{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given that line& ${L}_{1}$~passes through& $2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$~and parallel to& $3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$

and~line& ${L}_{2}$~passes through& $2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$~and parallel to& $\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$.

Then,~${a}_{1} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{1} = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$~and& ${a}_{2} = 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{2} = \overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

Shortest distance between lines is given by,~$d = \left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) \cdot \left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right)\left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right|$.

Now,~$\left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 3 & - 1 & 2 \\ 1 & - 2 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right| = \sqrt{{3}^{2} + \left(- 1\right)2 + \left(- 5\right)2} = \sqrt{35}$

And,~$\left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right) = \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$

Putting these values, we get~$d = \dfrac{\left(3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right)}{35} = \dfrac{- 1 + 10}{35} = \dfrac{9}{35}$

questions.solution:
Given points$A ( - 1, 2, - 3 ) , B ( 5, 0, - 6 ) , C ( 0, 4, - 1 )$

Let, the vector $AD$is the internal bisector of $∠ BAC$, point $D$ lie on the side& $BC$.

Now, $AB = \sqrt{\left(- 1 - 5\right)2 + {2}^{2} + \left(- 3 + 6\right)2} = \sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = 7$

and, $AC = \sqrt{\left(- 1 - 0\right)2 + \left(2 - 4\right)2 + \left(- 3 + 1\right)2} = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$

We know that, the bisector of angle $∠ BAC$, divides the side $BC$ in ratio& $AB: AC$, i.e. $7: 3$

So, the coordinate of $D$ is& $\left(\dfrac{3 \times 5 + 7 \times 0}{3 + 7}, \dfrac{3 \times 0 + 7 \times 4}{3 + 7}, \dfrac{3 \times \left(- 6\right) + 7 \times \left(-1\right)}{3 + 7}\right) = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{14}{5}, - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)

Hence,$ the vector\overset{→}{AD} =$\dfrac{5}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{4}{5}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{1}{2}\overset{^}{k}

So,$ the $direction cosines are \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{2}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}, \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{5}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}$' $\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}

$ i . e . $\dfrac{25}{714}, \dfrac{8}{714}, \dfrac{5}{714}$

questions.q: If the projections of the line segment $\overset{→}{AB}$ on $XY, YZ$ and $ZX$ planes are $\sqrt{15}, \sqrt{46},$7$ respectively, then the projection of \overset{→}{AB}$ on $y -$axis is
questions.solution:
Let, the vector $\overset{→}{AB} = l\overset{^}{i} + m\overset{^}{j} + n\overset{^}{k}$

Projection on $XY$ plane is& \sqrt{l^{2} + m^{2}} = \sqrt{15} ⇒ l^{2} + m^{2} = 15... $\left(1\right)$

Projection on $YZ$ plane is \sqrt{m^{2} + n^{2}} = \sqrt{46}$⇒ m^{2} + n^{2} = 46... \left(2\right)

Projection on $ZX$ plane is& \sqrt{n^{2} + l^{2}} =7 ⇒ n^{2} + l^{2} = 49... \left(3\right)

Subtracting equation \left(2\right) from& equation& \left(3\right),

\left(l^{2} + n^{2}\right)- \left(n^{2} + m^{2}\right)$ =49 - 46 = 3 ⇒ l^{2} - m^{2} = 3 ⇒ $\left(l + m\right)\left(l - m\right)$ = 3$

$⇒ l + m = 3 and l - m = 1$

So, $l = 2, m = 1$
Hence, the projection of $\overset{→}{AB}$ on $y$-axis is $m = 1$

$

questions.q: Find the equation of the plane passing through the point $( 2, 1, 3 )$ and perpendicular to the planes $x - 2y + 2z + 3 = 0$ and $3x - 2y + 4z - 4 = 0.$
questions.solution:
We can conclude, the normal& to the plane ${S}_{1}$

i.e. $x - 2y + 2z + 3 = 0$ is& (say) $\overset{→}{r1} = \overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$
and the normal to the plane ${S}_{2}$

i.e. $3x - 2y + 4z - 4 = 0$ is (say) $\overset{→}{r2} = 3\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}$
So, the normal to the plane ${S}_{3}$ (which is perpendicular to the plane ${S}_{1} and {S}_{2}$)

is $\overset{→}{r3} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & - 2 & 2 \\ 3 & - 2 & 4\end{cases}\right| = - 4\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}$

So, the equation of plane ${S}_{3}$ is

$- 4x + 2y + 4z + c = 0... \left(1\right)$

As, it is passing through the point $\left(2, 1, 3\right)$

So, substituting in equation $\left(1\right)$, we get,

$- 4 \times2 + 2 \times1 + 4 \times3 + c = 0 ⇒ - 8 + 2 + 12 + c = 0 ⇒ c = - 6$

Hence, the equation of the plane ${S}_{3}$ is

$- 4x + 2y + 4z - 6 = 0 or 2x - y - 2z + 3 = 0$

questions.q: The harmonic conjugate of $(2,3,4)$ with respect to the points $(3,-2,2)$ and $(6,-17,-4)$ is

& P=(2,3,4)

Let $P$ divides $A B$ in the ratio of $m: n$.

(2,3,4)=$\left[\frac{m(6)+n(3)}{m+n}, \frac{m(-17)+n(-2)}{m+n},\right.$\\
(2,3,4)=$\left[\frac{6 m(-4)+n(2)}{m+n}\right]$\\
$\frac{6 m+3 n}{m+n}=$2 \\
6 m+3 n=2 m+2 n \\
4 m=-n \\
$\frac{m}{n}=-\frac{1}{4}$\\
m: n=-1: 4
\end{gathered}

If point $P$ divides a line segment in the ratio of $m: n$, then its harmonic conjugate will divide same segment in the ratio of $-m: n\therefore$ Required ratio $=-m: n=1: 4\therefore$ Required harmonic conjugate

$\begin{aligned}$& =$\left(\frac{m x_2+n x_1}{m+n}, \frac{m y_2+n y_1}{m+n}, \frac{m z_2+n z_1}{m+n}\right)$\\

& =$\left(\frac{18}{5}, \frac{-25}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right)=\left(\frac{18}{5},-$5, $\frac{4}{5}\right)

questions.q: Two lines whose direction cosines are given by $a l+b m+c n=0$ and $f m n+g n l+h l m=0$ are perpendicular to each other if.........
questions.solution:
Let the direction cosines of lines are $l_1, m_1, n_1$ and $l_2, m_2, n_2$
Since, $a l+b m+c n=0$ and, $f m n+g n l+h m=0$
So, on eliminating ' $l$ ', we get

$\begin{gathered}$f m n+(g n+h m)$\left(-\frac{b m+c n}{a}\right)=$0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad a f m n=b h m²+c g n²+(b g+c h) m n=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad b h$\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)^$2+(b g+c h-a f)$\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)+$c g=0 $\text{ having }$\\
$\text{ roots } \frac{m_1}{n_1} \text{ and } \frac{m_2}{n_2} \text{, so }$\\
$\text{ product of roots }=\frac{m_1 m_2}{n_1 n_2}=\frac{c g}{b h}
\end{gathered}$Similarly on eliminating ' $m$ ', we get

$\begin{gathered}$g n l+(h l+f n)$\left(-\frac{a l+c n}{b}\right)=$0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad b g n l=a h l²+c f n²+(c h+a f) l n=0 \\
\Rightarrow a h$\left(\frac{l}{n}\right)^$2+(c h+a f-b g)$\left(\frac{l}{n}\right)+$c f=0 $\text{, having roots }$\\
$\frac{l_1}{n_1} \text{ and } \frac{l_2}{n_2} \text{, so product of roots } \frac{l_1 l_2}{n_1 n_2}=\frac{c f}{a h} .
\end{gathered}\because$ The lines are perpendicular.

$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore$& l_1 l_2+m_1 m_2+n_1 n_2=0 \\
\Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{c g}{b h}+\frac{c f}{a h}+$1\right) n_1 n_2=0 \Rightarrow $\frac{f}{a}+\frac{g}{b}+\frac{h}{c}=$0
\end{array}

questions.q: Angle between the lines of intersection of the planes \(x-y=0,2 x+y+z=0\) and \(2 x-z=0, x+y-3 z=0\) is
questions.solution:
Let the direction cosines of line of intersection of the planes \(x-y=0\) and \(2 x+y+z=0\) are \(a_1, b_1, c_1\) so
\(a_1-b_1=0\)
and \(2 a_1+b_1+c_1=0\)
By cross-multiplication method, we have
\($\frac{a_1}{-1-0}=\frac{-b_1}{1-0}=\frac{c_1}{1+2} \Rightarrow \frac{a_1}{1}=\frac{b_1}{1}=\frac{c_1}{-3}$
Similarly, let the direction cosines of line of intersection of the planes \(2 x-z=0\) and
$\begin{aligned}$x+y-3 z & =0 $\text{ are }$a_2, b_2, c_2 $\text{ so, }$\\
2 a_2-b_2 & =0 \\
a_2+b_2-3 c_2 & =0
\end{aligned}\)
By cross-multiplication method, we have
\($\frac{a_2}{3-0}=\frac{-b_2}{-6-0}=\frac{c_2}{2+1} \Rightarrow \frac{a_2}{1}=\frac{b_2}{2}=\frac{c_2}{1}$
So angle ' \($\theta$ ' between lines having directions cosines \(a_1, b_1, c_1\) and \(a_2, b_2, c_2\) respectively. is
$\begin{aligned}\theta$& =\cos ^{-1}$\left(\frac{   \left|$a_1 a_2+b_1 b_2+c_1 c_2\right|}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2} \sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}\right)$\\
& =\cos $^{-1} $\left(\frac{1+2-3}{\sqrt{1+1+9} \sqrt{1+4+1}}\right)\\
& =$\cos ^{-1}$(0)=90^{{}^{\circ}}
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (d) is correct.$

questions.q: \(\mathbf{A B}=\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{A C}=\mathbf{b}\) are the sides of \(\mathbf{a} \triangle A B C . P\) is a point on \(\mathbf{A B}\) and \(Q\) is a point on \(\mathbf{B C}\) such that \($\frac{A P}{P B}=\frac{1}{2}$\) and \($\frac{B Q}{Q C}=\frac{1}{2}$\). If the point of intersection of \(\mathbf{A Q}\) and \(\mathbf{C P}\) is \(D\) and the area of \(\triangle B C D\) is 7 square units, then the area of the \(\triangle A B C\) (in the same sq units) is
questions.solution:
According to given informations,
$\mathbf{A P}=\frac{\mathbf{a}}{3} \text{ and } \mathbf{A Q}=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{3}\)
Let \(D\) divides the line \(\mathbf{A Q}\) in ratio \(\lambda: 1\) and \(\mathbf{C P}\) in \(\mu: 1\).
So, \(\quad=\frac{\lambda(2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})}{3(\lambda+1)}=\frac{\mu \frac{\mathbf{a}}{3}+\mathbf{b}}{\mu+1}\)
On comparing
\begin{array}{rlrl}& & \frac{\mu}{3(\mu+1)}& =\frac{2 \lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \text{ and } \frac{1}{\mu+1}=\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)}\\
\Rightarrow & \frac{\mu}{3(\mu+1)}& =\frac{2}{\mu+1} \Rightarrow \mu=6 \\
\text{So, }& \frac{1}{7}& =\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \Rightarrow3 \lambda+3=7 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{4}\\
\Rightarrow & & \text{ AD }& =\frac{2 a+\mathbf{b}}{7}
\end{array}$
So, $\frac{1}{7}=\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \Rightarrow3 \lambda+3=7 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{4}\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{A D}=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{7}\)
Now area of \(\triangle B C D=\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{B C} \times \mathbf{B D}|\)
\begin{aligned}& =\frac{1}{2}\left|(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \times\left(\frac{\mathbf{b}-5 \mathbf{a}}{7}\right)\right|\\
& =\frac{1}{14}|(-\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a})-(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})|\\
& =\frac{4}{14}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|=7 \text{ (given) }
\end{aligned}$
\(\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|=\frac{49}{4}$\)
\(\Rightarrow\) Area of \(\triangle A B $C=\frac{49}{4}$\)
Hence, option (a) is correct.

 \text{ and }  =\left|\frac{2-3}{\sqrt{2} \sqrt{29}}\right|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{58}}

Hence, option (c) is correct.

If the point $P ( \alpha, \beta, \gamma )$ lies on the plane $2x + y + z = 1$ and~

$\left[\begin{cases}\alpha & \beta & \gamma\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & 9 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 & 1\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right],$ then ${α}^{2} + {β}^{2} + {γ}^{2} =$
questions.solution:
Since, point $P\left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right)$ lies on the plane therefore, it satisfy the equation of plane and therefore we have

$2\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 . . . \left(i\right)$

Now, we have,

$\left[\begin{cases}\alpha & \beta & \gamma\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & 9 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 & 1\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{cases}\alpha + 8\beta + 7\gamma & 9\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma & \alpha + \beta + \gamma\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right]$

Hence,

$\alpha + 8\beta + 7\gamma = 0 . . . \left(ii\right)9\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma = 0 . . . \left(iii\right)\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0 . . . \left(iv\right)$

Subtracting $\left(iv\right)$ from $\left(i\right)$, we get

$\alpha = 1$

Putting in $\left(iii\right) \text{ and } \left(iv\right)$, we get

$2\beta + 3\gamma = - 9 . . . \left(v\right)$

$\beta + \gamma = - 1 . . . \left(vi\right)$

On solving, we get $\gamma = - 7 \text{ and } \beta = 6$

Therefore,

${\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {\gamma}^{2} = 86$

Similarly, vector equation of line joining& $OC & OD$

& $= \overset{→}{a} - 2\overset{→}{b} + 3\overset{→}{c} + s \left(-4\overset{→}{b} + 3\overset{→}{c}\right)$

$= \overset{→}{a} + \left(-2 - 4s\right)$\overset{→}{b} + $\left(3 + 3s\right)$\overset{→}{c} . . . $\left(ii\right)$

$⇒ s = - 1$

Substituting these values in $\left(i\right)$, we get

$\overset{→}{r} = \overset{→}{a} + 2\overset{→}{b}$&

questions.solution:
We know that, if a line makes an angle& $\alpha, \beta & \gamma$~with positive direction of& $X - \text{axis}, Y - \text{axis} & Z - \text{axis}$~then

${cos}^{2}\alpha + {cos}^{2}\beta + {cos}^{2}\gamma = 1 . . \left(i\right)

Now, given angles are~$\alpha = {tan}^{- $1}\sqrt{$7}$~and& $\beta = {tan}^{- 1} $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{3}}\right)$.

Then,~

$cos\left({tan}^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{7}\right)\right) = cos\left({cos}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

$cos\left({tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)\right) = cos\left({cos}^{- 1} \left(\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right) = \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}

Therefore, from~\left(i\right), we get

$⇒ $\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$2 + $\left(\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$2 + {cos}^{2}\gamma =1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{3}{8} + {cos}^{2}\gamma =$1$

$⇒ {cos}^{2}\gamma =1 - $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ {cos}^{2}\gamma = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ cos\gamma = \pm $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ \gamma = $\dfrac{π}{4}\text{or}\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

So, the normal vector for the required plane is $\overset{→}{n} = 9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}$

Equation of required plane,

$⇒ \overset{→}{r} $\cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) =27 + 15 + \dfrac{63}{2}

$⇒ $\left($ x\overset{^}{i} + y\overset{^}{j} + z\overset{^}{k}\right)$\cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) =42 + \dfrac{63}{2}

$⇒ 9x + 3y + $\dfrac{9}{2}$ z = $\dfrac{147}{2}

$⇒ 6x + 2y + 3z = 49$.

Plane passing through the line of intersection of planes $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}=1$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{m}=-4\mathbf{r} \cdot(\mathbf{n}+\lambda \mathbf{m})=1-4 \lambda($ where $\lambda$ is a scalar quantities)

\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) $\cdot(2 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$} & +\hat{$\mathbf{k}$}) \\
& +\lambda(\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) $\cdot(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=0 \\

\end{aligned}$ So, required plane is,

$\begin{gathered}
\mathbf{r} \cdot\left[2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \frac{-11}{3}(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}})\right]=1-4\left(\frac{-11}{3}\right)$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\mathbf{r} \cdot\left(\frac{-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}}{3}+\frac{2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}}{3}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right)=\frac{47}{3}$\\
(x \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+y \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+z \hat{$\mathbf{k}$}) $\cdot(-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+12 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=47 \\

questions.q: If $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are vectors of equal magnitude such that $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})=\alpha,(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})=\beta,(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a})=\gamma$, then the minimum value of $\cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$ is
questions.solution:
We have, $\cos \alpha=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}, \cos \beta=\frac{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}|}$ and $\cos \gamma=\frac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{c}||\mathbf{a}|}$ Also, it is given that $|\mathbf{a}|=|\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{c}|=\lambda$ (say), where $\lambda > 0$. Then, $\cos \alpha=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lambda^2} ; \cos \beta=\frac{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{\lambda^2}$ and $\cos \gamma=\frac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{\lambda^2}\Rightarrow \cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}$
We know that, \begin{aligned}$& |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|^2=(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})\\ = & {\left[|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2+|\mathbf{c}|^2+2(\mathbf{a} $\cdot $\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b}$ \cdot $\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c}$ \cdot $\mathbf{a}$)\right]$} \\ \Rightarrow & {\left[\lambda^2+\lambda^2+\lambda^2+2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a})\right] \geq0 } \\ & \quad\left[\because|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|^2 \geq 0\right] \\ \Rightarrow & 2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \geq-3 \lambda^2 \end{aligned} $\\ Now, from $Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get \begin{aligned} \cos\alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$& \geq $\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\left(-\frac{3}{2}$ \lambda^2\right)$ \\ & =-\frac{3}{2}$\end{aligned}Thus, the $minimum value of \cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$ is $-\frac{3}{2}$.

Mid-point of line segment joining the points $P(3,2,4)$ and $Q(-1,0,-2)$ is $R(1,1,1)$ and direction ratios of line segment $P Q$ is $4,2,6$, so direction ratios of normal to the plane is \langle a, b, c\rangle=\langle 4,2,6\rangle. So, equation of plane will be 4 x+2 y+6 z+d=0 Since, plane (i) bisect the line segment joining $ P Q$.
So, $\quad d=-12$
Therefore, $\quad a c+b d=0$.

questions.q: If the vertices of a $\triangle A B C$ are $A=(2,3,5)$, $B=(-1,3,2), C=(3,5,-2)$, then the area of the $\triangle A B C$ (in sq. units) is
questions.solution:
The vertices of $\triangle A B C$ are $\begin{aligned}& A=(2,3,5), B=(-1,3,2), C=(3,5,-2) \\
& \text{ So, } \mathbf{A B}=(-1-2) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(3-3) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(2-5) \hat{\mathbf{k}}=-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
& \mathbf{A C}=(3-2) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(5-3) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(-2-5) \hat{\mathbf{k}}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-7 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
& \text{ Now, }|\mathbf{A B} \times \mathbf{A C}|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
-3 & 0 & -3 \\
1 & 2 & -7
\end{array}\right| \\
& =\hat{ \mathbf{i} }(0+6)-\hat{ \mathbf{j} }(21+3)+\hat{ \mathbf{k} }(-6+0) \\
& =6 \hat{ \mathbf{i} }-24 \hat{ \mathbf{j} }-6 \hat{ \mathbf{k} } \\
& \text{ Now, }|\mathbf{A B} \times \mathbf{A C}|=\sqrt{(6)^2+(-24)^2+(-6)^2}$\\
& =$\sqrt{36+576+36}$\\
& =$\sqrt{648}=18 \sqrt{2}$\\
& \therefore $\text{ area$ of $} \triangle$ A B C=$\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{A B} \times \mathbf{A C}|$\\
& =$\frac{1}{2} \times18 \sqrt{2}$\\
& =9 $\sqrt{2} \text{ sq. units. } \\
&
\end{aligned}
$

questions.q: If a line makes angles $\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{7}, \tan ^{-1} \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}$ with $X$-axis, $Y$-axis respectively, then the angle made by it with $Z$-axis is
questions.solution:
A line makes angle $\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{7}$ and $\tan ^{-1} \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}$ with $X$-axis and $Y$-axis respectively.
So,
Sc $\begin{aligned}& \alpha=\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{7}\\
& \tan \alpha=\sqrt{7}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \cos \alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\\
& \text{ and }\\
& \beta=\tan ^{-1} \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}\\
& \tan \beta=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \cos \beta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{8}}\\
&
\end{aligned}
  \\ Let angle make with $Z$-axis is $\gamma$. So, \begin{aligned}& \cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=1 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{8}}\right)+\cos ^2 \gamma=1 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{4}{8}+\cos ^2 \gamma=1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2}+\cos ^2 \gamma=1
\end{aligned} \begin{array}{lr}
\Rightarrow& \cos ^2 \gamma=\frac{1}{2}\\
\Rightarrow & \cos \gamma= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\
\Rightarrow & \cos \gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ or } \frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\\
\Rightarrow & \gamma=\frac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } \pi-\frac{\pi}{4}\\
\Rightarrow & \gamma=\frac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } \frac{3 \pi}{4}
\end{array}$ So, angle made by line with $Z$-axis is $\frac{\pi}{4}  and  \frac{3 \pi}{4}$.

questions.q: If a non-zero vector a is parallel to the line of intersection of the plane determined by the vectors $\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}, 3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and the plane determined by the vectors $2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}, \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$, then the angle between the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ is
questions.solution:
Normal of the plane $P_1$ determined by the vectors $\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$,
$$
\mathrm{n}_1=[(\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}) \times(3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})]=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 3 & -2
\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathbf{i}}
$$
Normal of the plane $P_2$ determined by the vectors $2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{n}_2=[(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}})] \\
& =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
2 & 3 & 0 \\
1 & -3 & 0
\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathbf{i}}(0)-\hat{\mathbf{j}}(0)+\hat{\mathbf{k}}(-6-3)=-9 \hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{aligned}
$$
Since, $a$ is parallel to the line of intersection of planes $P_1$ and $P_2$.
$$
a= \pm\left(n_1 \times n_2\right) \quad= \pm\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -9
\end{array}\right|= \pm 9 \hat{\mathbf{j}}
$$
Now, angle $\theta$ between $9 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos \theta= \pm\left(\frac{9}{9 \sqrt{3}}\right)= \pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\
\therefore \quad & \theta=\cos \left( \pm \frac{}{\sqrt{ }}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Given that, in $\triangle A B C, L, M, N$ are points on BC, $\mathrm{CA}$ and $\mathrm{AB}$ respectively, dividing in the ratio $1: 2,2: 3 and 3: 5$. Also, point $K$ divides A B$ in the ratio 5: 3$.
Now, according to the section formula, $\begin{aligned}& L=\frac{2 \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}}{3}, M=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+3 \mathbf{c}}{5}\\ & N=\frac{3 \mathbf{b}+5 \mathbf{a}}{8}, K=\frac{5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}}{8}\\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{AL}}=\frac{2 \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}}{3}-\mathbf{a}=\frac{2 \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}-3 \mathbf{a}}{3}\\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{BM}}=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+3 \mathbf{c}}{5}-\mathbf{b}=\frac{2 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{c}-5 \mathbf{b}}{5}\\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{CN}}=\frac{3 \mathbf{b}+5 \mathbf{a}}{8}-\mathbf{c}=\frac{3 \mathbf{b}+5 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c}}{8}\\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{CK}}=\frac{5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}}{8}-\mathbf{c}=\frac{5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c}}{8}\\ & \because \quad \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AL}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{BM}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CN}}}{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CK}}} \mid= \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \left|\frac{\frac{2 \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}-3 \mathbf{a}}{3}+\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+3 \mathbf{c}-5 \mathbf{b}}{5}+\frac{3 \mathbf{b}+5 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c}}{8}}{\frac{5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c}}{8}}\right| \\ = & \left|\frac{(5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c})}{15(5 \mathbf{b}+3 \mathbf{a}-8 \mathbf{c})}\right|=\frac{1}{15}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The cartesian equation of the plane whose vector equation is $\gamma=(1+\lambda-\mu) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(2-\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(3-2 \lambda+2 \mu) \hat{\mathbf{k}}$ where $\lambda, \mu$ are scalars, is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \gamma=(1+\lambda-\mu) \hat{i}+(2-\lambda) \hat{j}+(3-2 \lambda+2 \mu) \hat{k} \\
& =\hat{i}+\lambda \hat{i}-\mu \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\lambda \hat{j}+3 \hat{k}-2 \lambda \hat{k}+2 \mu \hat{k} \\
& =(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2 \hat{k})+\mu(-\hat{i}+2 \hat{k})
\end{aligned}$
Equation of plane is given by
$\{r-(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})\}+[(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2 \hat{k}) \times(-\hat{i}+2 \hat{k})]=0\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & \{r-(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})\} \cdot(-2 \hat{i}-\hat{k})=0 \\
\Rightarrow & r(2 \hat{i}+\hat{k})-5=0 \\
\Rightarrow & r(2 \hat{i}+\hat{k})=5
\end{array}
Now, equation of plane in cartesian form
\begin{aligned}
& (x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}) \cdot(2 \hat{j}+\hat{k})=5 \\
& \therefore \quad 2 x+z=5
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:

From eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & r=3(2 r+3 q)+4 q \\ & r=6 r+9 q+4 q \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 5 r=-13 q \Rightarrow r=\frac{13}{5} q \Rightarrow|r|=\frac{13}{5}|q| \end{aligned}\therefore \quad r$ and q have opposite directions Hence, $|r| > 2|q|$

questions.solution:
Given that, line makes angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ with the four diagonals of a cube, then we know that
$\begin{aligned}
& \cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma+\cos ^2 \delta=\frac{4}{3} \\
& \text{ Since, } \cos ^2 \theta=1-\sin ^2 \theta \\
& 1-\sin ^2 \alpha+1-\sin ^2 \beta+1-\sin ^2 \gamma+1-\sin ^2 \delta=\frac{4}{3} \\
& \therefore \quad \sin ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \gamma+\sin ^2 \delta=4-\frac{4}{3}=\frac{8}{3}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $M_1, M_2, M_3$ and $M_4$, are respectively the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{a}_2=-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$, $\mathbf{a}_3=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{a}_4=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$, then the correct order of $M_1, M_2, M_3$ and $M_4$ is
questions.solution:
Given that, $a_1=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}\begin{aligned}
& a_2=3 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}-4 \hat{k} \\
& a_3=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\
& a_4=-\hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}
\end{aligned}$
As $M_1, M_2, M_3 and M_4$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathrm{a}_1, \mathrm{a}_2, \mathrm{a}_3$ and $\mathrm{a}_4$ respectively.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad M_1=\left|\mathrm{a}_1\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(2)^2+(-1)^2+(1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt{6} \\
& M_2=\left|\mathrm{a}_2\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(3)^2+(-4)^2+(-4)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{9+16+16}=\sqrt{41} \\
& M_3=\left|\mathrm{a}_3\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(-1)^2+(1)^2+(-1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt{3} \\
& M_4=\left|\mathrm{a}_4\right|
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& =\sqrt{(-1)^2+(3)^2+(-1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{1+9+1}=\sqrt{11}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, the correct order of magnitudes
$M_3 \lt  M_1 \lt  M_4 \lt  M_2$

Let the coordinates of four points $P, Q, R and S$ be $(3,-4,5), \quad(0,0,4), \quad(-4,5,1) \quad$ and $\quad(-3,4,3)$ respectively.

Equation$ of line R S$ is

\Rightarrow & & 3 r_1+r_2 & =7 \\
$\text{$ and }& & -r_2+5 & =4 r_1-4 \\
\Rightarrow & & 4 r_1+r_2 & =9
\end{aligned}

On subtracting Eq. (iv) from Eq. (iii), we get

r_1=2

On putting the value of$ r_1 in $Eq. (iii), we get

3(2)+r_2=7 \Rightarrow r_2=1

So, required point$ of intersection is(-3,4,3)$ i.e.,

-3 $\mathbf{i}+4  \mathbf{j}+3 \mathbf{k} $

The given lines are $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}_1+\lambda \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}_2+\mu  \mathbf{b}_2  where,

\begin{aligned}& \mathbf{a}_1=3 \mathbf{i}+5 \mathbf{j}+7 \mathbf{k}, \mathbf{b}_1=\mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\
& \mathbf{a}_2=-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}, \mathbf{b}_2=7 \mathbf{i}-6 \mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\
& \quad\left|\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right|=\left|$\begin{array}{ccc}
$\mathbf{i}$& $\mathbf{j}$ & $\mathbf{k}$ \\
1 & 2 & 1 \\
7 & -6 & 1
\end{array}$\right| \\
\Rightarrow \quad & | \mathbf{i} (2+6)- \mathbf{j} (1-7)+ \mathbf{k} (-6-14)| \\
\Rightarrow & |^{8}  \mathbf{i}+6   \mathbf{j}-$20 $\mathbf{k}$ | \\
\Rightarrow & \sqrt{64+36+400}=\sqrt{500}=10 \sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}$ Now,

 \begin{aligned}& {\left[\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right) \mathbf{b}_1 \mathbf{b}_2\right]=\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right)} \\
& =(-4 \mathbf{i}-6 \mathbf{j}-8 \mathbf{k}) \cdot(8 \mathbf{i}+6  \mathbf{j}-20 \mathbf{k} ) \\
& =-32-36+160 \\
& =160-68=92
\end{aligned} 

Shortest distance

 \begin{aligned}& =\frac{\left[\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right)\right]}{\left|\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right|}\\
& =\frac{92}{10 \sqrt{5}}=\frac{46}{5 \sqrt{5}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}, \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}, \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$. A vector in the plane of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ has projection $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ on c. Then, one such vector is

and $l+2 m+3 n=0\ldots$ (ii)
From Eq. (ii), $l=-(2 m+3 n)$ Using in Eq. (i), we get
$-3(2 m+3 n) m+4(2 m+3 n) n+m n=0\Rightarrow \quad-6 m^2-9 m n+8 m n+12 n^2+m n=0\Rightarrow \quad-6 m^2+12 n^2=0$
Now, $m^2=2 n^2 \Rightarrow m= \pm \sqrt{2} n$
Now, $\quad m=\sqrt{2} n\Rightarrow \quad l=-(2 \sqrt{2} n+3 n)=-(2 \sqrt{2}+3) n\therefore l: m: n=-(3+2 \sqrt{2}) n: \sqrt{2} n: n=-(3+2 \sqrt{2}): \sqrt{2}: 1$
Also, $\quad m=-\sqrt{2} n \Rightarrow l=-(-2 \sqrt{2}+3) nl: m: n=-(3-2 \sqrt{2}) n:-\sqrt{2} n: n=-(3-2 \sqrt{2}):-\sqrt{2}: 1$
If $\theta$ is the angle between the lines, then
$\cos \theta=\frac{l_1 l_2+m_1 m_2+n_1 n_2}{\sqrt{l_1^2+m_1^2+n_1^2} \sqrt{l_2^2+m_2^2+n_2^2}}=\frac{(3+2 \sqrt{2})(3-2 \sqrt{2})+(\sqrt{2})(-\sqrt{2})+1.1}{\sqrt{(3+2 \sqrt{2})^2+(\sqrt{2})^2+1^2}{\sqrt{(3-2 \sqrt{2})^2+(-\sqrt{2})^2+1^2}}}=\frac{9-8-2+1}{\sqrt{9+8+12 \sqrt{2}+2+1} \sqrt{9+8-12 \sqrt{2}+2+1}}=0\Rightarrow \cos \theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\cos \frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A plane $\pi$ makes intercepts 3 and 4 respectively on $Z$-axis and $X$-axis. If $\pi$ is parallel to $Y$-axis, then its equation is :
questions.solution:
Given that $a=4, c=3$
Equation of the plane ' $\pi$ ' is
$\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}+\frac{z}{b}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{b}+\frac{z}{3}=1$
Since, $\pi$ is parallel to $Y$-axis.
$\therefore \quad \frac{0 \cdot \frac{1}{a}+1 \cdot \frac{1}{b}+0 \cdot \frac{1}{c}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}+\frac{1}{c^2}}}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{b}=0$
Thus, the equation of plane $\pi$ is
$\frac{x}{4}+\frac{z}{3}=1 \Rightarrow 3 x+4 z-12=0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the plane passing through $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-1)$ and perpendicular to $2 x-y+z+5=0$ is :
questions.solution:
Let the equation of plane passing through $(1,1,1)$ is
$a(x-1)+b(y-1)+c(z-1)=0\ldots$ (i)
It is also passing through $(1,-1,-1)$.
$\therefore \quad a(0)+b(-2)+c(-2)=0$
or $b+c=0\ldots$ (ii)
Since, Eq. (i) is perpendicular to the plane
$2 x-y+z+5=0\therefore \quad 2 a-b+c=0\ldots$ (iii)
Since, Eqs. (ii) and (iii) are identical
$\therefore \quad \frac{a}{-2-2}=\frac{b}{-4-0}=\frac{c}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{a}{-4}=\frac{b}{-4}=\frac{c}{4}\therefore$ Required equation of plane is
$x+y-z-1=0$

questions.q: The acute angle between the two lines whose direction ratios are given by $l+m-n=0$ and $l^2+m^2-n^2=0$, is
questions.solution:
Given that

l+m-n=0

and

l²+m²-n²=0

From equaion (i) $l=-(m-n)$
Putting in equation (ii), we get

$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow$& (m-n)^2+m²-n² & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & m²+n²-2 m n+m²-n² & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & 2 m²-2 m n & =0 \\
& 2 m(m-n) & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & m=0, m & =n
\end{aligned}$ From equation (i), ifm=0$, then

l=n \Rightarrow l: m: n=1: 0: 1

If $m=n$, then $l=0 \Rightarrow l: m: n=0: 1: 1$
If $\theta$ is the acute angle, then

$\begin{aligned}
\cos\theta$& =$\left|\frac{1.0+0.1+1.1}{\sqrt{1+1} \sqrt{1+1}}\right|=\frac{1}{2}=\cos \frac{\pi}{3}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\theta$& =$\frac{\pi}{3}
\end{aligned}$

$We know that,
